item.title: Goal drift: how a multi-agent crew ends up solving a different problem
item.description: Loop drift is one agent staying busy without getting closer to done. Hand the same failure to a crew and every agent stays busy, produces defensible work, and the team’s collective objective still ends up somewhere your original request never sent it — a genuine multi-agent goal drift failure mode, not a mistake in any single agent’s reasoning. A concrete feature-build failure, the four things that make a goal decay one handoff at a time, and what to measure so a ‘done’ check compares against the original ask instead of the nearest upstream spec.

item.title: Split-brain: when multi-agent memory consensus quietly fails
item.description: In distributed systems, split-brain is what happens when a partition convinces two halves of a cluster that each is the sole leader, and both start accepting writes. Multi-agent systems build the identical topology every time more than one agent reads and writes a ‘shared’ memory store with no lock, no leader, and no version check — and the failure that follows is a genuine multi-agent memory consensus problem, not a bug in any one agent. The mechanism, a concrete incident-response failure, and what to instrument before it costs you a duplicate action.

item.title: Failure modes in multi-agent teams: how a crew of agents breaks differently
item.description: A single agent fails by getting the task wrong. A team of agents fails in ways no single agent can: correlated collapse, diffused responsibility, context fragmentation, and consensus that converges on nothing. The four failure modes that only exist once you have more than one agent — and why adding agents can lower reliability.
